title: 2 Kings 6:24–33
context: 2 Kings 6:24–33 begins the account of Ben-hadad’s siege of Samaria, which continues in chapter 7. Famine becomes so severe that a donkey’s head and a small measure of dove’s dung sell for high prices. A woman cries out to the king, and he answers that if the LORD does not help, he cannot. She then tells of two mothers who agreed to eat their sons, and of how her son was eaten while the other woman hid hers. The king tears his clothes and is seen to be wearing sackcloth, yet he swears to kill Elisha. Elisha, sitting with the elders, anticipates the messenger, and the unit ends with words blaming the LORD for the evil. The text records the horror plainly, and many interpreters connect it with the covenant curses on siege (Deuteronomy 28:52–57; compare Lamentations 4:10). Both traditions read the passage soberly as showing the depth of Israel’s distress and the king’s failure to turn to the LORD in faith.

verses.text: After this, Benhadad king of Syria gathered all his army, and went up and besieged Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes: Ben-hadad king of Syria gathers his whole army and besieges Samaria. Arminians see the end of the brief peace and a new crisis for Israel, which tests the king and people once more.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Interpreters discuss the chronology of this siege in relation to the peace of 6:23, and the text gives no explicit time. Both traditions read the verse as the beginning of a crisis that continues into chapter 7.

verses.text: There was a great famine in Samaria. Behold, they besieged it until a donkey’s head was sold for eighty pieces of silver, and the fourth part of a kab of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver.
verses.arminianNotes: Famine in Samaria is so severe that a donkey’s head sells for eighty pieces of silver and a fourth of a kab of dove’s dung, about a pint, for five. Arminian readers see the desperate prices as a measure of Israel’s suffering under siege.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. The phrase "dove’s dung" may refer to the actual substance or to a plant known by that name, and interpreters discuss both. Both traditions read the verse as showing the extreme conditions in the city.

verses.text: As the king of Israel was passing by on the wall, a woman cried to him, saying, “Help, my lord, O king!”
verses.arminianNotes: As the king walks on the wall, a woman cries out, "Help, my lord, O king!" Arminians see a desperate appeal from one of the king’s people, which tests whether he can or will help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the king walking the wall as a picture of a ruler surrounded by suffering he cannot relieve. Both traditions read the verse as introducing a tragic encounter.

verses.text: He said, “If the LORD doesn’t help you, where could I get help for you? From the threshing floor, or from the wine press?”
verses.arminianNotes: The king answers that if the LORD does not help her, he cannot help her from the threshing floor or the wine press. Arminian readers see the king admitting his helplessness but speaking with bitterness rather than faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that his words are true, yet he does not turn to the LORD in prayer or repentance. Both traditions read the verse as showing a king who recognizes God’s power but does not trust him.

verses.text: Then the king asked her, “What is your problem?” She answered, “This woman said to me, ‘Give your son, that we may eat him today, and we will eat my son tomorrow.’
verses.arminianNotes: The king asks what is wrong, and she says another woman proposed that they eat her son that day and the other woman’s son the next. Arminians read the verse soberly as showing how far the siege had driven people, a fulfillment of the covenant warnings in Deuteronomy 28:53–57.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the account with grief and restraint, as the text presents it. Both traditions see the horror as a sign of covenant judgment and avoid using it as a spectacle or illustration.

verses.text: So we boiled my son and ate him; and I said to her on the next day, ‘Give up your son, that we may eat him;’ and she has hidden her son.”
verses.arminianNotes: She says they boiled and ate her son, but the next day the other woman hid her son. Arminian readers see the text recording a horror plainly, without comment, and they treat it as evidence of the depth of Israel’s distress under judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and read the verse with sorrow rather than elaboration. Both traditions connect it with the covenant curses and with Lamentations 4:10, and they see the narrative calling for repentance rather than curiosity.

verses.text: When the king heard the words of the woman, he tore his clothes. Now he was passing by on the wall, and the people looked, and behold, he had sackcloth underneath on his body.
verses.arminianNotes: The king tears his clothes, and the people see that he is wearing sackcloth underneath. Arminians see outward signs of mourning and perhaps repentance, but they note that the king’s next words show he does not turn to God in faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the sackcloth as a hidden sign of distress, not necessarily true repentance, since the next verse blames Elisha. Both traditions read the verse as showing a king overwhelmed by the crisis.

verses.text: Then he said, “God do so to me, and more also, if the head of Elisha the son of Shaphat stays on him today.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king swears to have Elisha beheaded that day. Arminian readers see him blaming God’s prophet for the crisis, perhaps because Elisha had counseled patience, and they see this as anger against God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the king’s oath as turning against the very prophet who had saved him before (6:9–10). Both traditions read the verse as showing how suffering can harden rather than soften a heart that does not trust God.

verses.text: But Elisha was sitting in his house, and the elders were sitting with him. Then the king sent a man from before him; but before the messenger came to him, he said to the elders, “Do you see how this son of a murderer has sent to take away my head? Behold, when the messenger comes, shut the door, and hold the door shut against him. Isn’t the sound of his master’s feet behind him?”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha sits with the elders and tells them the king, "this son of a murderer," has sent to take his head, and they should hold the door shut. Arminians see God giving Elisha knowledge of the threat, as he had known the Syrian plans earlier.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Many interpreters understand "son of a murderer" as referring to the king’s descent from Ahab, whose house was guilty of Naboth’s death (1 Kings 21). Both traditions see God protecting his prophet in a dangerous moment.

verses.text: While he was still talking with them, behold, the messenger came down to him. Then he said, “Behold, this evil is from the LORD. Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?”
verses.arminianNotes: The messenger arrives, and the speaker says, "Behold, this evil is from the LORD. Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?" Arminian readers see despair that has given up on God, and they note it is unclear whether the messenger or the king is speaking.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree that the speaker is uncertain and see words that acknowledge God’s sovereignty but reject waiting on him. Both traditions read the verse as leading into Elisha’s promise of relief in chapter 7, where God answers despair with mercy.
